body.text: Kashmir Chand’s two-room tin-roofed house stands on an 18-marla (1 marla=272.25 square feet) plot in Jammu and Kashmir’s Reasi district, about 35 kilometres from the renowned Vaishno Devi shrine, in a settlement described in official records as a “colony”. There is a small kitchen, a courtyard, and a dilapidated bathroom near the entrance. That is all that remains of the economic security of a family that once owned and cultivated 12 kanals of land about 25 years ago (1 kanal=0.125 acre).
“When we had land, we used to store enough food rations for 7-8 months at home,” said Chand (70). “Now, if we do not work for a day, we do not know about tomorrow.”

When the land was forcibly acquired in 2000, villagers like him who resisted the displacement faced police action, and first information reports were lodged against several protesters. The consequences of the dispossession and displacement have unfolded now. “Once we had adequate land, livestock, fruit trees, and a big house. Now, we have just two rooms,” said Chand, whose son works as a contractual/casual employee at the Jal Shakti Public Health Engineering Department, earning about Rs.9,000 a month.

Nearly a kilometre away from this colony stand the symbols of the modern expansion of the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board, including a university, a super-speciality hospital, a medical college (whose recognition was revoked in January 2026), residential infrastructure, and other institutions. The infrastructure has been built on vast swathes of land that once sustained over 250 farming families from Kakryal village and the adjoining Sirah Kotla village, situated over 35 km from the cave shrine.

In the first half of 2026 alone, the cave shrine in the Trikuta Hills attracted over 50 lakh devotees. While donations to the shrine climbed from Rs.63.85 crore in 2020-21 to Rs.231.50 crore in 2023-24, according to reports, pilgrim offerings of gold and silver have also risen sharply.

Since taking over the management of the shrine from the local Baridar community in 1986, the Shrine Board has transformed the pilgrimage into one of India’s best-managed religious journeys. It has developed extensive infrastructure for the convenience of pilgrims, including upgraded tracks, accommodation, a community kitchen, proper sanitation, medical facilities, and other amenities along the route, while expanding its footprint beyond the shrine. It even runs a helicopter service, offering an eight-minute flight from Katra to Sanjichhat that spares the pilgrims a gruelling 14-km trek to the mountain shrine.
Well-managed pilgrimage
The success of this pilgrimage model has resulted in an unprecedented boom in Katra town’s economy and the overall tourism industry of Jammu and Kashmir.

However, for the families of these two villages, located about 10 km from Katra town, the spectacular success of the pilgrimage model is a painful paradox. Everyone in this colony narrates the same stories of having lost agricultural self-sufficiency, regular income, food security, economic independence, a secure home and property rights, an asset that could be passed to the next generation, and most importantly, social status.

A sizeable section of residents at the colony today sells physical labour, doing menial jobs in the Shrine Board’s infrastructure built on their land, for sustenance.

Many residents complained to Frontline that despite working for more than eight hours a day, they were not getting enough wages to make ends meet. Many families deplored the fact that they were even deprived of government welfare schemes.

The land transfer to the Shrine Board’s project was backed by the coercive power of the state in pursuit of what the law recognised as a “public purpose”. In 2000, when Reasi was part of the erstwhile Udhampur district, the Jammu and Kashmir government headed by the then Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah invoked its compulsory acquisition powers under the Jammu and Kashmir Land Acquisition Act, 1990, which was applicable then, to allocate assemble more than 6,000 kanals or 750 acres for establishing a residential and a technical university (2,631 kanals and 14 marlas in Sirah Kotla and approximately 3,760 kanals in Kakryal).
The project was created under The Jammu and Kashmir Shri Mata Vaishno Devi University Act, 1999, passed by the State legislature, and funded by the Shrine Board.

Among other facilities, a Delhi Public School branch was established in 2006 on the campus by the Maharaja Hari Singh Social and Education Foundation, which is owned and managed by a direct descendant of Maharaja Hari Singh.

Subsequently, the Shrine Board set up the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Narayana Superspeciality Hospital. Operated by Narayana Health under a public-private partnership, the hospital claims to offer concessional care, providing completely free emergency treatment to Vaishno Devi pilgrims, free outpatient department consultations to residents of four surrounding villages, and cashless complex surgeries through the Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY) scheme.

According to sources, Narayana Health manages operations and retains the business revenue and operational surplus, while the Shrine Board acts as a philanthropic sponsor, subsidising the hospital’s charitable and free treatment mandates rather than seeking a commercial profit.

Yet, 25 years after their forced displacement, the residents of the two villages remain embroiled in litigation. The legal battle of villagers from Sirah Kotla seems to have run its course. The dispute went through several stages of litigation. The District Collector initially fixed rates at Rs.25,000 per kanal for cultivable land, Rs.15,000 for Banjar kadim (long-standing uncultivated) land, and Rs.10,000 for Gair Mumkin (uncultivable) land.
Locked in litigation

In 2008, the Court of the Principal District Judge, Udhampur, enhanced the rates to Rs.1.5 lakh, Rs.50,000, and Rs.30,000 respectively. On the university administration’s appeal, however, the Jammu and Kashmir High Court, in June 2024, reduced the rate for cultivable land to Rs.85,000 per kanal while retaining Rs.50,000 for Banjar kadim and Rs.30,000 for Gair Mumkin land, besides granting 15 per cent jabrana (solatium).

The university’s subsequent review petition was dismissed on July 25, 2024, with the court holding that its plea was essentially an attempt to reopen issues already decided. The university then took the matter to the Supreme Court through a special leave petition. However, the petition was dismissed/disposed in October 2024.

Likewise, in the case of Kakryal, the Collector initially awarded the same rates for the three categories. The Court of the Principal District Judge, Udhampur, enhanced the rates in 2013 to Rs.1 lakh for the first and Rs.50,000 for the other two categories.

In the view of high court’s direction to deposit the award amount in all the cases with Registrar Judicial of the court within two weeks, the court granted several opportunities to the university to deposit the awarded amount.

Kapil Sharma (45), an advocate, said: “Despite repeated directions, the university administration has flagrantly violated the direction given by the court. The university proposed out-of-court negotiations within a framework of Rs.75,000 per kanal for cultivable land and Rs.40,000 for the other two categories. But the issue is yet to be resolved fully despite several court rulings.” Sharma has been spearheading the high court battle for affected families. His father lost 70 kanals of agricultural land in Kakryal village to the university project.
In both cases, while the enhanced amounts were reportedly paid to a section of claimants, the disputes involving co-ownership, fragmented titles, and rehabilitation benefits remain unaddressed.

Following the revocation of Articles 370 and 35A in 2019, the Central Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, should have automatically applied to the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, alongside other Central laws.

According to Kapil Sharma, the displaced families have been deprived of its benefits. Section 24 of the Act determines how pending land acquisition proceedings initiated under the older framework are handled.

“The provision clearly states that the new law applies if the government has neither taken physical possession of the land nor deposited the compensation money. We are trapped in a legal vacuum. The new Central land acquisition law has been held inapplicable to our case because of the Supreme Court’s 2022 ruling in Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Nisar Ahmed Ganai & Ors. The apex court determined that the Central Act cannot (retroactively) apply to acquisitions initiated under the old Jammu and Kashmir State Land Acquisition Act.”

Left without the protection of the Central law, the landowners now seemingly face the university’s blatant disregard for judicial orders, as the acquiring authorities have failed to release even the court-mandated enhanced compensation.

“The university administration lured a few individuals and managed to get out-of-court agreements signed with the assurance that they will get the agreed amount of settlement instantly. Those who accepted the offer were desperate due to their economic vulnerabilities. They were even denied mandatory solatium of 15 per cent under the old law. As per Section 30 (1) of the Central law, they are legally entitled to 100 per cent solatium,” said Sharma.

“Now, we are tired… it seems we won’t get justice. Despite knowing fully that the farmers have lost everything, the university has stalled payouts as part of a calculated financial strategy. The university is weaponising inflation to actively devalue the compensation owed to displaced landowners,” he added.

On the university’s obligations towards displaced families, P.V. Rajagopal, a noted Gandhian and land rights expert, said: “A university must create knowledge that directly addresses the needs of the poorest in the society. Students cannot remain unaware of their immediate surroundings while learning about distant regions. It is meaningless if your knowledge has no relevance to the lives of the people around you.”

Rajagopal, founder president of Ekta Parishad, a movement to fight for the rights of the oppressed, pointed to a growing number of cases where local communities lose land to disguised “public trusts” that actually serve private or corporate interests.
University let-down
He said there was an urgent need to establish fast-track courts at the district and tehsil levels to ensure timely resolution of land-related disputes.

“For poor and marginalised communities, the conventional legal process is often too expensive and time-consuming. Even when they approach the courts, they may lack the resources to sustain prolonged litigation. This structural inequality frequently allows more powerful parties to prevail in land disputes,” he added.
On March 1, 2003, the university executive council passed a resolution on rehabilitation benefits and the potential allotment of residential plots for completely displaced families.

Accordingly, it provided 120 kanals to about 250 families for residential purpose. Each claimant was allotted a plot of 18 marlas and one shop site measuring one marla adjacent to the acquired land at Rs.9,000 for the residential plot and Rs.5,000 for the shop site. More than two decades later, those original households have grown into multiple families, creating an acute housing shortage.

The displaced families, who got plots, rued that they do not have legal ownership rights or official papers such as an allotment letter, lease deed, revenue mutation, title document, and terms of transfer. “They can vacate us from this land anytime. We cannot mortgage our plot for even a bank loan,” said Girdhari Lal (62), who suffers from hypertension.

Ashok Kumar (58) told Frontline, “We are two brothers and two sisters. We owned 19 kanals of land, but the total compensation was split between us, leaving each of us with just Rs.4.5 lakh. Can anyone truly rebuild their life with that amount?”
“I am a daily wage labourer with at least six family members depending on me. Still, the authorities refuse to issue a below poverty line ration card in my name,” he said.

Ved Raj (44), an advocate, said that his father’s family comprising three brothers had over 100 kanals of ancestral land besides claim over 50 kanals of shamlat (common) land. Originally from Kakryal, Raj fought a long-drawn legal battle for enhanced compensation in the Court of the Principal District Judge, Udhampur, representing 150 displaced families.

“At the time of our forcible eviction, our joint family got a paltry compensation of Rs. 70 lakh, while only one brother got a plot for house construction,” said Raj, who practices in the Udhampur district court.
“There are many families which didn’t get any help from the university or the government for building houses. Today, one can’t buy one kanal for even Rs.1 crore near the university,” he added.
The rehabilitation policy tried to address the immediate displacement of one generation without anticipating the needs of the generations that followed.

Ongoing litigation has also exposed a critical fault line in the rehabilitation debate, with the High Court ruling in Shri Mata Vaishno Devi University v. Pritam Singh and Others (2024), which states that providing residential and commercial plots constitutes a voluntary rehabilitation measure. The university argued that it had allotted displaced families plots for houses and shops. The High Court, however, held that this rehabilitation measure could not be treated as a substitute for, or adjustment against, the compensation payable for compulsorily acquired land.

“The Shrine Board’s modern institutional legacy was built not on the pilgrimage alone but also on the land of Sirah and Kakryal. It must empower the people on whose land this legacy was built,” said Ved Raj.

Under the Jammu and Kashmir Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Act, the Lieutenant Governor of Jammu and Kashmir serves as the ex-officio chairperson of the Shrine Board and nominates distinguished members from different fields to it. But the law does not have a statutory provision for representation of displaced landowners or directly affected communities.

The legal character of the Shrine Board itself reflects an interesting constitutional position. In a recent judgment, in Subash Raina Vs State of J&K & Ors, the Jammu and Kashmir High Court observed that while the Shrine Board is not “state” within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution, it nevertheless performs public functions and, in appropriate cases involving public law, can be subject to judicial review.

In 2023, the Supreme Court quashed the acquisition of approximately 6,000 acres of land along Odisha’s Puri-Konark Marine Drive for the Anil Agarwal Foundation’s proposed Vedanta University project. The apex court ruled that the land acquisition process was illegal, driven by favouritism, and violated Article 14 of the Constitution. It directed the State government to return the land to local families.

In the past 20-30 years, observers have noticed a regular trend in high courts. Many courts accepted petitions against changes in the titles of village common land or agricultural land. The State governments had given this land to private trusts to build deemed universities at very cheap rates. However, many projects violated rules, skipped public consultations, or failed to get environmental clearances. Owing to such irregularities, the high courts routinely cancelled the projects.
In November 2025, the Supreme Court initiated reviews and nationwide audits to examine how private educational institutions obtain preferential treatment, government backing, and land concessions.

“The question arises as to why private universities need such vast tracts of land,” said Rajagopal. He wanted to know whether the land acquired in the name of education was subsequently used consistently with the purpose stated in the acquisition proceedings.
Shortchanged landowners

Meanwhile, the displaced farming families near the Vaishno Devi shrine suffer from a lack of expected jobs, educational reservation, and scholarships for their children, while their medical coverage remains severely restricted. “Our children should have received reservation in the Shrine Board’s educational institutions, alongside the promised employment opportunities, but nothing has materialised so far,” said Tilak Raj (73), a resident of Sirah, demanding meaningful rehabilitation and jobs for the affected families.

“Ideally, every member of a displaced household should be entitled to free medical treatment at the Shrine Board’s hospital. Currently, the hospital caps medical coverage at just Rs.1 lakh, and limits it strictly to the primary titleholders, the men in whose names the compensation cheques were issued, and their wives. Many of them have passed away, and the next generation doesn’t get this benefit,” he added.

He also raised the issue of fruit trees, arguing that villagers were never adequately compensated for the loss. “The university administration influenced the horticulture department to compensate on the basis of old rates that were fixed in 1964,” he claimed, and complained that the entire compensation process had resulted in significant financial losses for villagers, leaving them feeling exploited.

Babli Devi (48), who ekes out a living working as a domestic help, expressed deep anxiety over the future. “I have three daughters and no son. I’m worried how I will marry them off.”

Experts said that the crucial question in this context was if “public purpose” ends once compensation is paid or whether, decades later, the institutions built on land forcibly acquired still owe something to the local communities that made them possible.

“If people are making huge profit by running universities, running hospitals, running a religious institution and all that profit, at least 2 per cent can be ploughed back into the community that lost their land. Even from a corporate social responsibility point of view, these people who lost their land need not be suffering so much,” said Rajagopal.

The majority of the original landowners from Sirah Kotla and Kakryal were small farmers with limited formal education and little experience navigating courts, revenue records, and acquisition procedures. That lack of knowledge and institutional power impacted their ability to contest compensation and rehabilitation decisions, Ved Raj said.
“Our lives have become miserable after losing the land. We are ready to return what we received from the university as financial compensation. Give us back our land,” he added.
(Frontline had sent a detailed questionnaire by email to the university administration, but they had not responded to it as of September 15.)
